title: What Is Man? God's Majesty and Human Dignity
summary: Framed by the refrain “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth”, this hymn praises God whose glory fills the heavens and who silences his enemies through the praise of children. Looking up at the moon and stars, David marvels that God cares for human beings at all, and then marvels again that God has crowned them with glory and set them over his works.
story: After a run of laments, Psalm 8 is the first hymn of pure praise in the Psalter, and it lifts the reader's eyes from the troubles of David's enemies to the night sky. It is also the Psalter's meditation on Genesis 1. The creation account said that God made humanity in his image and gave them rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and every creature on the land. Psalm 8 turns that account into a song. Coming after Psalm 2, which spoke of God's anointed king ruling the nations, and after the cries of Psalms 3 to 7, it reminds the reader what human beings were made for: not to be crushed by enemies, but to rule God's world under him.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David. Some readers have imagined the young shepherd under the stars before he became king, but nothing in the text or heading names an occasion. The psalm could have been sung in many settings, and its concerns are universal rather than tied to a particular event. Scholars who date the headings later still generally regard the psalm as an early hymn of Israel's worship.

The background that matters most is the world Israel shared with its neighbors. In Mesopotamia and Egypt, the sun, moon, and stars were worshiped as gods or linked with them, and royal ideology placed the king, not ordinary people, closest to the gods. Psalm 8 treats the heavenly bodies as the work of God's fingers, and it gives the royal language of glory, honor, and rule to humanity as such.
cultural:
The heading's “According to Gittith” is obscure. The word may refer to an instrument or tune associated with the Philistine city of Gath, or, as some ancient translators understood it, to wine presses and the vintage season. It also heads Psalms 81 and 84.

The psalm is full of royal imagery that a first reader would have recognized. Glory and honor are the qualities of kings. Crowning is what happens at a coronation. Putting enemies or subjects under one's feet was a familiar picture of dominion in the ancient world, where kings were depicted with conquered foes beneath them. Verse 2 pictures infants and nursing babies, the weakest members of society, as the ones through whom God establishes his strength against his foes. In a world that prized military power, that reversal is striking. Verses 7 and 8 list the animals in the categories of Genesis 1: domestic herds, wild beasts, birds, and sea creatures, including whatever swims the paths of the sea.
literary: Psalm 8 is a hymn, and its shape is simple and beautiful. The same refrain opens and closes it (verses 1 and 9), an envelope structure scholars call an inclusio, so that everything said about human beings sits inside the praise of God's name. Human glory is real but derived. The center of the psalm is the question of verse 4, set in parallel lines: “what is man”, “the son of man”. Both phrases mean a human being, with an emphasis on frailty; the Hebrew word enosh in the first line often suggests weakness and mortality. The psalm then moves from smallness to dignity, from the vast heavens to the creatures under humanity's feet, in a descending order that mirrors the order of creation.

outline.t: Heading and refrain: how majestic is your name
Praise from infants silences God's enemies
Under the night sky: what is man?
Crowned with glory and set over God's works

doctrines.note: The heavens are the work of God's fingers, and the moon and stars are set in place by him. Nothing in the sky is divine, and the vastness of creation is a witness to the greatness of its maker.

Human beings are small and frail, yet God is mindful of them and has crowned them with glory and honor as rulers over his works. The psalm holds both truths together: humility before God and dignity under him.
The psalm begins and ends with God's name, meaning his revealed character and reputation. Human rule is exercised inside God's greater majesty and for his praise.

words.note: Enosh, man or mankind. A poetic word for human beings that often carries overtones of weakness and mortality (Psalm 103:15 says that the days of enosh are like grass). Its use in verse 4 heightens the wonder: God is mindful of creatures so frail.

Paqad, to visit or attend to, rendered “care for” in verse 4. The verb means to pay close attention to someone, whether in blessing or in judgment. When God visits Sarah (Genesis 21:1) he gives her a son. Here the point is that God does not merely know that human beings exist; he takes personal notice of them.

Elohim, usually God, but here in verse 5 it can mean heavenly beings. The Hebrew says that God made humanity a little lower than elohim, and translations divide between “God” and “the angels” or “heavenly beings”. The Greek translation chose angels, and Hebrews 2:7 follows it. Either way, human beings are placed just below the heavenly realm, at the top of the visible creation.

Mashal, to rule. The verb is used of kings and governors. Verse 6 restates the commission of Genesis 1:26-28 in royal terms: human beings rule God's works as stewards under him, not as owners in their own right.

christ: The New Testament reads Psalm 8 as a psalm about humanity that finds its fulfillment in Jesus. Hebrews 2:6-9 quotes verses 4 to 6 and observes that we do not yet see everything subject to human beings, but we do see Jesus, made for a little while lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because he suffered death. Paul applies the words about everything under his feet to the risen Christ in 1 Corinthians 15:27 and Ephesians 1:22. In Matthew 21:16, when children cry out praise to Jesus in the temple, he answers his critics with verse 2 in its Greek form, which speaks of praise prepared from the mouths of infants. Jesus is presented as the true human being, who does what Adam was made to do. The phrase “son of man” here simply means a human being; Jesus' favorite title for himself draws chiefly on Daniel 7:13, though Christians have seen the two uses as related.

hard.q: Does the psalm give human beings license to exploit the natural world?
hard.a: Critics have sometimes argued that biblical language of dominion encouraged the careless use of nature. The psalm itself points another way. Human rule is framed on both sides by the praise of God's name, so it is delegated rule, exercised under the real owner. The model of kingship in Israel's law was a king who served under God's instruction and did not exalt himself over his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:14-20), and the Old Testament elsewhere requires care for animals and land (Exodus 23:10-12; Deuteronomy 25:4; Proverbs 12:10). Christians differ on how to weigh environmental questions today, but the psalm's picture is stewardship that brings glory to the creator, not license to consume his works.

questions: When have you felt small before the size of the universe? How does verse 4 speak to that feeling?
Verse 5 says God has crowned human beings with glory and honor. How would it change how you treat the people you find hardest to respect?
What would faithful rule over the works of God's hands look like in your daily work, home, and use of creation?
